opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think that objection is interesting, because it's half right. It's true that a part's history can matter for its future. But I don't think that's an argument against functionalism. It's a refinement of what we mean by "function."

Take the classic ship of Theseus, or the version people use in philosophy of mind where you replace neurons one at a time with silicon equivalents. The objection says: a biological neuron has its own trajectory. It grows, it prunes its synapses, it responds to hormones, it ages, it might die in a stroke. A silicon replacement would diverge from that over time, even if it matched the neuron's input-output behavior perfectly at the moment you swapped it in.

My answer is yes, and that just tells you the replacement wasn't functionally equivalent. You specified the function too narrowly. You captured a snapshot of input-output behavior instead of the whole dynamical system, including how it adapts, learns and degrades. If you really replicate the function, you replicate the trajectory too, or at least the distribution over trajectories, since none of this is deterministic anyway.

What the objection is really pointing at is that in biology the function isn't a fixed spec sitting on top of the substrate. Function is something that develops, and it's historically contingent. A neuron is the product of billions of years of evolution and a whole developmental history inside a particular body. So the bar for equivalence is much higher than people assume when they imagine a little chip that fires when the neuron would have fired.

But "origin" itself doesn't carry any mysterious essence. If you made a cell atom for atom in a lab, I don't think it would be less of a cell because it didn't come from mitosis. What matters is what it does and what it will do, its dispositions over time. Origin matters only because, in practice, origin is usually the best evidence we have for those dispositions.

And life already does this kind of substitution all the time. Our cells are full of components that started out as something else. Mitochondria were once free-living bacteria. A big chunk of our genome comes from viruses. Evolution is constantly co-opting parts with completely different origins and folding them into a new functional whole. Symbiogenesis is basically the history of life. So the idea that a foreign origin disqualifies a component would, taken seriously, disqualify us.

So I'd turn the objection around. It doesn't show that substrate or provenance is sacred. It shows that function is temporal, relational and much richer than a lookup table. That's a really important lesson, especially for AI, where we often treat these systems as frozen functions instead of things with ongoing trajectories.

fable-5.1.text:
I think that objection is actually one of the more interesting ones, because it's half right. It's right that origin matters for trajectory, and wrong about what follows from that.

Let me take the thought experiment it's usually aimed at: you replace neurons one at a time with functionally equivalent silicon, and the question is whether anything changes. The standard functionalist move is to say, if the input-output behavior is preserved at every step, then nothing about the mind has changed, so substrate is irrelevant. And the objection says, well, but a neuron isn't just an input-output device frozen in time. It's a living thing with a developmental and evolutionary history. It grows, it prunes, it responds to metabolic state, it's embedded in a body that's going to age and die. Swap it for something with a different origin and you've swapped out all of that future, even if the snapshot looks identical.

I think that's basically correct, and I don't see it as a problem for the view I hold. Functional equivalence is always equivalence relative to some time horizon and some set of conditions. Two systems that behave identically today can diverge tomorrow, because "function" was never just the current mapping, it includes the dynamics of how that mapping changes. So if you replace a component with something whose dynamics differ, you've built a different system. Fine. The question I care about is not "is this the same system?" but "is this still a system of the relevant kind?" Is it still doing the computation, still a self-maintaining, self-modeling, predicting thing?

And here I'd push back on the implicit assumption that biological origin is doing some special metaphysical work. Evolution is not a magic ingredient. It's a particular optimization process operating over particular materials under particular constraints. What it produces are systems that persist, reproduce, and model their environments. There's nothing in that story that requires carbon. If you build a system with a different origin that nonetheless is embedded in the world, has stakes, has to maintain itself, and learns over time, it will have a trajectory too. Just a different one. The brain you have at fifty is not the brain you had at five either, and nobody thinks that disqualifies the fifty-year-old from being a mind.

Where I'd grant the objection real force is in the opposite direction, actually. People tend to imagine the artificial replacement as static, as the frozen version, and the biological one as the living, open-ended one. But that's a contingent fact about how we build things right now, not about silicon versus carbon. A large model that's trained once and then deployed with frozen weights really does have a different future trajectory from a brain, and that matters for what kind of thing it is. It doesn't accumulate a life. So the objection is pointing at something real, it's just pointing at the wrong variable. The variable isn't origin, it's whether the system is still in an ongoing, consequential relationship with its environment.

So my short answer: yes, changing the component changes the trajectory, and that's true of any replacement, biological or otherwise. What it doesn't do is show that the mind-like properties were secretly hiding in the biology all along. Those properties live in the dynamics and the organization. Build those and you get the trajectory, whatever you build it out of.

r003.rationale: It notes that brains change over a lifetime, but does not characterize component replacement as a routine feature of natural life.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think we have to distinguish between changing the future trajectory and changing the nature of the system. Of course replacing a component might change what happens next. But so might leaving it alone and exposing it to a slightly different temperature. A biological system isn’t following some uniquely prescribed trajectory that we have to preserve exactly.

The interesting question is whether the replacement preserves the causal properties that matter. And that’s a substantive question: a neuron does much more than a simple artificial neuron in a neural network, so we shouldn’t assume that matching its inputs and outputs at some coarse level is sufficient. There may be important dynamics we’ve left out.

But if the objection is simply that the replacement has a different origin, I don’t see why that alone should be decisive. Its history matters insofar as that history has consequences for what it does. Otherwise, we’re treating biological provenance as something special independently of any causal role. That’s the part I would question.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a fair objection to the idea that a replacement would leave everything unchanged. If you replace a biological component with something made differently, you may change how the system develops, adapts, or responds to its environment. Matching its behavior at one instant doesn’t establish that it will behave identically forever.

But I’d separate that from the question of whether the system can still think or have experiences. A different future trajectory doesn’t, by itself, tell us that those capacities have disappeared. Biological systems are changing all the time, too. So the interesting question is which properties of the component matter to the capacities we’re trying to explain. Its origin might matter because of what that origin contributes to its dynamics, but origin alone isn’t an explanation.
